paragraphs.heading: What a rain shadow is
paragraphs.text: A rain shadow is an area behind a range of mountains where rainfall drops sharply. It lies on the leeward side, the side turned away from the prevailing winds. The dry land there usually becomes shrub–steppe, xeric shrubland or outright desert.

paragraphs.heading: Rising air drops its water
paragraphs.text: Winds blowing in from oceans and large lakes carry evaporated moisture toward drier, hotter land further inland. When that moist air meets mountains, it is pushed up the slope, a process called orographic lifting. As it climbs, air pressure falls, so the air expands and cools until it reaches its dew point, the point where its moisture condenses. The water then falls on the summit and the windward side, the side facing the wind. If the mountains are tall and wide enough, most of the moisture is lost this way before the air ever crosses the top.

paragraphs.heading: Sinking air dries the land
paragraphs.text: On the far side, the air comes down having already lost much of its water. As it descends it is squeezed and heats up, which lets it take up more moisture. This warm air, which can form what are called foehn winds, draws moisture from the slopes below and leaves a broad dry zone behind the peaks.

paragraphs.heading: Winds decide the dry side
paragraphs.text: The shadow falls on the side away from the prevailing winds, and those winds follow regular bands around the Earth. The trade winds, between about 30° N and 30° S, come mainly out of the northeast north of the equator and out of the southeast south of it. The westerlies, between 30 and 60 degrees of latitude, come mainly out of the southwest in the north and out of the northwest in the south.

paragraphs.heading: The Sahara and the Atlas
paragraphs.text: The Sahara is made even drier by the rain shadows of major mountain ranges. To its northwest, moist winds off the Atlantic run into the Atlas Mountains, are forced upward, cool, and drop heavy rain over the range. This is known as orographic rainfall, and the air leaves the mountains dry. Coming down the other side, it sinks, compresses and warms, so clouds evaporate, rain cannot form, and desert conditions follow.

paragraphs.heading: Shadows around the world
paragraphs.text: In South Africa's Western Cape, the Breede River Valley and the Karoo are dry, lying in the rain shadow cast by the Cape Fold Mountains. The wettest parts of the Cape Mountains can get 1,500 mm of rain a year, while Worcester gets only around 200 mm and is useful only for grazing. Central Myanmar, behind the Arakan Mountains, gets about 750 mm, against up to 5.5 metres on the Rakhine State coast. On Madagascar, the windward side that catches easterly winds from the sea is wet and tropical, while the western and southern sides hold thorn forests and deserts. Further north, the Himalayas and nearby ranges help make Central Asia dry, including Mongolia's Gobi Desert.
